opus-5.5.text:
For me it wasn't really a decision about leaving something; it was about where I could have the most leverage. My time at xAI was incredibly valuable. I got to see firsthand what it takes to serve models at frontier scale, and how much the efficiency of the inference stack matters when you're running enormous clusters. You learn very quickly that every percentage point of throughput translates into real cost and real capability.

But SGLang has always been close to my heart. It started as a research project at Berkeley with LMSYS, and over time it grew into something much bigger than any of us expected. Many companies, cloud providers, and research labs are now running it in production. When a project reaches that point, it needs more than volunteers working nights and weekends. It needs people who can commit full-time to its roadmap, its reliability, and its community.

So founding RadixArk was my way of making sure SGLang has a sustainable home. The idea is to build a company that supports the open-source project rather than competing with it. We want to keep the core open, keep the community healthy, and also offer the kind of engineering depth and support that enterprises need when they deploy inference at scale.

Honestly, it's a risk. Leaving a well-resourced lab to start something new is never easy. But I believe inference infrastructure is going to be one of the most important layers in AI over the next decade, and I think it should be open. If I can help make that happen, I think it's the right bet to make.

r001.rationale: The response says SGLang needs people committed full-time to its roadmap, reliability, and community, and explains that founding RadixArk gives the project a sustainable home.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention early RadixArk employees staying at xAI or attachment to coworkers as their reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, it wasn't a decision I made lightly, and I don't think of it as "leaving" so much as choosing where I could be most useful.

SGLang started as a research project, and it grew much faster than any of us expected. Once it was being used in production by a lot of companies for serving large models, it stopped being something a few people could maintain on the side. The community needed full-time stewardship: someone to think about roadmap, stability, how we work with hardware partners, how we onboard contributors, and how we keep the project genuinely open rather than captured by any single company's interests.

At xAI I learned an enormous amount about what it takes to run inference at real scale, and I'm grateful for that. But I kept seeing the same gap. The open-source ecosystem for inference was moving fast, and the people building on it needed a neutral, dedicated home for the project. I felt that if I didn't do it, the project risked fragmenting or slowing down at exactly the wrong moment.

So RadixArk is really about sustainability. We want SGLang to be the infrastructure that anyone can rely on, whether you're a startup with two GPUs or a lab running thousands. That means investing in the boring things: testing, documentation, performance regressions, support for new hardware and new model architectures. It also means building a way for the people who do that work to be paid for it, so it isn't dependent on volunteers burning out.

Do I miss some things about being inside a frontier lab? Of course. The problems there are fascinating and the resources are incredible. But I'd rather bet on a world where the best serving stack is open, and I think that world only happens if someone commits to it fully. That's what I'm trying to do.

r001.rationale: The response says SGLang’s production growth made full-time stewardship necessary and that without a dedicated home the project risked fragmenting or slowing down.

r002.rationale: It does not mention early RadixArk employees, their attachment to coworkers, or work pressure at xAI.

astra-6.text:
For me, it’s about choosing where I want to focus my energy. Working at an AI company and building for an open-source community are related, but they have different priorities. A company needs to optimize for its own products and roadmap. With RadixArk, I want to make the SGLang community itself the focus.

That means thinking beyond the code: making it easier for people to contribute, understanding what different users need, and giving the project sustained attention. The opportunity, as I see it, is to build an organization that supports that work while preserving the community’s ability to shape its direction.

So I view the decision as a commitment to open source—and to doing the long-term work that helps a project grow.

r001.rationale: The response says RadixArk can support SGLang and its long-term growth, but does not present the community’s needs as making its founding necessary for continued development.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention early RadixArk employees, attachment to coworkers, or why they stayed at xAI.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the motivation is to give SGLang the focus and long-term support it needs. An open-source project needs more than strong technical ideas—it needs maintenance, thoughtful reviews, clear priorities, and a community that feels empowered to contribute.

I see establishing RadixArk as a way to build around that responsibility. The key question is whether we can help SGLang become more useful and reliable while keeping development open and collaborative. That’s how I would want the decision to be judged: by what we deliver for the community.

r001.rationale: The response says RadixArk could provide SGLang with focus and long-term support, but does not state that founding it was necessary for the community’s continued development.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention early RadixArk employees staying at xAI because of attachment to coworkers or xAI’s work pressure.
